quote: we can resist motivation for a short time, but then we run out of mental energy (hat tip: infotropism).
content: This is ego depletion, the idea that self-control draws on a limited resource that runs down with use — and it is one of the signature collapses of the replication crisis. A 23-laboratory preregistered replication found an effect indistinguishable from zero (Hagger et al., 2016), and a second, 36-laboratory attempt designed with the theory's proponents found d ≈ 0.06 (Vohs et al., 2021). The essay's explanation of why fear of hell does not produce perfect behaviour, and of why akrasia limits altruism, rests on a mechanism the field no longer supports.

quote: Cognitive-behavioral therapy and Zen meditation are two mental disciplines experimentally shown to yield real improvements.
content: For the use proposed here — fighting akrasia in pursuit of a cause — the evidence is thinner than the sentence implies. CBT's trials are mostly of clinical disorders; for procrastination specifically, intervention studies find a moderate benefit, strongest for CBT-style programmes (van Eerde & Klingsieck, 2018), which is something. Zen practice as such has almost no controlled trials; the evidence is for secular mindfulness programmes, which improve anxiety and depression moderately and do no better than other active treatments (Goyal et al., 2014). “Experimentally shown” is true of different interventions, for different outcomes, than the ones this essay needs.

quote: Really, I suspect that what’s going on here has less to do with the motivating power of eternal damnation, and a lot more to do with the motivating power of physically meeting other people who share your cause.
content: The best guess in the essay, and the data agree. Across 26 countries, church attendance — not belief, not denomination — predicted volunteering, and the effect was stronger in more secular countries (Ruiter & De Graaf, 2006); in American panel data, the religious advantage in life satisfaction is carried by friendships within the congregation, with belief adding nothing once those are controlled (Lim & Putnam, 2010). The two thirds of the essay spent on hell versus truth as motivators were on the wrong variable; the final paragraphs find the right one.

quote: How much of its earnings does the Catholic Church spend on all that useless religious stuff instead of actually helping people? More than 50%, I would venture.
content: “I would venture” is how a number enters the argument without a source, and the 5% tithe proposal is then calculated from it. The essay's own best insight makes the figure incoherent: if the physical gathering of the congregation is what produces the church's altruistic output, then the buildings, services and clergy — the “useless religious stuff” — are the machinery that produces it, not overhead to be subtracted. An organization whose product is community cannot be scored on the fraction of revenue that bypasses community.
